rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj treat al-insī and al-anāsī as a singular-plural pattern like kursī/kirāsī.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والزجاج : الإنسي والأناسي كالكرسي والكراسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adjective is singular despite a plural sense: faʿīl can denote abundance, as in 25:38 and 4:69.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل كثيرين لأنه قد جاء فعيل مفردا ويراد به الكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jurists derive water rulings from its description as purifying, asking whether water purifies and whether other liquids do too.
rows.anchor: استنبطوا أحكام المياه من قوله تعالى : { وأنزلنا من السماء ماء طهورا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unchanged water is pure in itself and purifies others, except that jurists dispute the status of water already used.
rows.anchor: فهو طاهر في ذاته مطهر لغيره ، إلا الماء المستعمل

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī considers used water pure but not purifying.
rows.anchor: فإنه عند الشافعي طاهر وليس بمطهر

rows.speaker: مالك والثوري
rows.claim: Mālik and al-Thawrī permit ablution with used water.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك والثوري يجوز الوضوء به

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: In a report through Abū Yūsuf, Abū Ḥanīfa regards used water as impure.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة في رواية أبي يوسف إنه نجس

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī argues that the Prophet prohibited bathing in still water while in major ritual impurity; otherwise the water would remain purifying and the prohibition would lack purpose.
rows.anchor: لا يغتسل أحدكم في الماء الدائم وهو جنب

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: He reasons that Companions did not save water used on journeys despite needing water later; if it still purified, they would have kept it.
rows.anchor: الصحابة كانوا يتوضؤون في الأسفار وما كانوا يجمعون تلك المياه

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik invokes 25:48 and 8:11: water's purifying quality should persist after use under the presumption that an established status remains.
rows.anchor: فدلت الآية على حصول وصف المطهرية للماء ، والأصل في الثابت بقاؤه

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik reads ṭahūran as allowing purification with the water repeatedly.
rows.anchor: قوله : { طهورا } يقتضي جواز التطهر به مرة بعد أخرى

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik argues that the unrestricted washing command in 5:6 is fulfilled by used water, since washing means running liquid over a limb.
rows.anchor: واستعمال كل المائعات غسل ، لأنه لا معنى للغسل إلا إمرار الماء على العضو

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: A poetic line uses washing for tears cleansing eyeliner, evidence for the broad sense of washing.
rows.anchor: فياحسنها إذ يغسل الدمع كحلها

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Because bathing with used water performs the commanded washing, Mālik argues it fulfills the obligation.
rows.anchor: فمن اغتسل بالماء المستعمل فقد أتى بالغسل ، فوجب أن يكون مجزئا له

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet wiped his head with leftover water in his hand after ablution.
rows.anchor: توضأ فمسح رأسه بفضل ما في يده

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet used moisture from his beard to wipe his head after ablution.
rows.anchor: توضأ فأخذ من بلل لحيته فمسح به رأسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that after bathing the Prophet found a dry patch, then used damp hair to wet it.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أنه عليه السلام : ( اغتسل فرأى لمعة في جسده

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik analogizes used water to pure water that touches a pure body, as when water touches stone or iron.
rows.anchor: ماء طاهر لقي جسدا طاهرا فأشبه ما إذا لقي حجارة أو حديدا

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: He compares it with water used in a fourth rinse or for cooling and cleaning, not in a ritual obligation.
rows.anchor: الماء المستعمل في الكرة الرابعة والمستعمل في التبرد والتنظيف

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Water running from the upper face to an unwashed lower part still suffices there although it has washed the upper part.
rows.anchor: إذا وضع الماء على أعلى وجهه وسقط به فرض ذلك الموضع

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī adduces the verse and beard-moisture report to show that used water is pure.
rows.anchor: ومن السنة أنه عليه السلام : أخذ من بلل لحيته ومسح به رأسه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says water is created pure and nothing makes it impure unless its taste, smell, or color changes; no grading is supplied.
rows.anchor: خلق الماء طهورا لا ينجسه شيء إلا ما غير طعمه أو ريحه أو لونه

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī argues that the Prophet's ablution splashed water on him, yet no one was reported to wash or change clothes, establishing consensus it is not impure.
rows.anchor: ولا شك أنه أصابه ما تساقط منه ، ولم ينقل أنه غير ثوبه ولا أنه غسله

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī again analogizes used water touching a pure body to water touching stone.
rows.anchor: ماء طاهر لقي جسما طاهرا فأشبه ما إذا لاقى حجارة

rows.speaker: أصحاب الشافعي
rows.claim: Shāfiʿī's associates unanimously say water used in an obligatory act of worship does not purify.
rows.anchor: المستعمل فيما كان فرضا وعبادة فهو غير مطهر باتفاق أصحاب الشافعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Water used for a required act that is not worship is exemplified by a Muslim man's dhimmī wife bathing after menstruation so intercourse becomes permissible.
rows.anchor: الماء الذي استعملته الذمية التي تحت الزوج المسلم

rows.speaker: أصحاب الشافعي
rows.claim: For water used in nonobligatory worship—second or third washes, renewed ablution, recommended baths—Shāfiʿī's associates hold two positions.
rows.anchor: فلأصحاب الشافعي في هذين القسمين وجهان

rows.speaker: أصحاب الشافعي
rows.claim: Water used for a fourth wash or cooling and cleaning is unanimously not classified as used and remains pure and purifying.
rows.anchor: فذاك باتفاق أصحاب الشافعي غير مستعمل ، وهو طاهر مطهر

rows.speaker: أصحاب الشافعي
rows.claim: The soundest Shāfiʿī position treats water from a garment's second and third washes as purifying when one wash removed the impurity.
rows.anchor: فالمنفصل في الكرة الثانية والثالثة مطهر على الأصح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Water changed by long standing remains suitable for ablution; the Prophet reportedly used the well of Buḍāʿa.
rows.anchor: المتغير بطول المكث فيجوز الوضوء به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Buḍāʿa well water is described as resembling henna infusion.
rows.anchor: وكان ماؤها كأنه نقاعة الحناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Water made foul-smelling by a nearby carcass that does not touch it remains purifying.
rows.anchor: وقع بقرب الماء جيفة فصار الماء منتنا بسببها فهو أيضا مطهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A pure substance touching water without mixing—oil, perfume, oud, amber, or solid camphor—does not remove its purifying status, by analogy with a nearby carcass and the verse's original ruling.
rows.anchor: المتغير بسبب وقوع الدهن والطيب والعود والعنبر والكافور الصلب فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unavoidable admixtures such as soil, mud, leaves, and algae leave water purifying: the verse establishes purity and avoiding these changes is difficult, which 22:78 relieves.
rows.anchor: لأن الطهورية ثبتت بالآية والاحتراز عن ذلك عسير ، فيكون مرفوعا لقوله : { ما جعل * عليكم فى الدين من حرج }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same ruling applies when water runs over or emerges from arsenic, lime, or kohl deposits.
rows.anchor: لو جرى الماء في طريقه على معدن زرنيخ أو نورة أو كحل

rows.speaker: أصحاب الشافعي
rows.claim: The correct Shāfiʿī position permits slight change from dispensable admixtures, such as saffron or flour, if water remains the name.
rows.anchor: جاز الوضوء به على الصحيح من المذهب ، لأنه لم يسلبه إطلاق اسم الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If extensive mixing gives water a new name such as broth, ablution is invalid by agreement.
rows.anchor: فإن استحدث اسما جديدا كالمرقة لم يجز الوضوء به بالاتفاق

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: If substantial mixing changes the water without creating a new name, al-Shāfiʿī disallows ablution while Abū Ḥanīfa permits it.
rows.anchor: فعند الشافعي لا يجوز الوضوء به

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī argues that the Prophet's prescribed ablution must use unchanged water, since the report that prayer is accepted only with this ablution cannot mean every altered water works.
rows.anchor: هذا وضوء لا يقبل الله الصلاة إلا به

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: If rosewater mixes with water, one cannot know whether limbs were washed with rosewater alone; doubt cannot remove certain ritual impurity, while an imperceptible trace counts as absent.
rows.anchor: فيحتمل أن بعض الأعضاء قد انغسل بماء الورد دون الماء

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī treats ablution as devotional, not rationally intelligible: rosewater fails while muddy, foul water works, so follow the text rather than analogy.
rows.anchor: الوضوء تعبد لا يعقل معناه ، فإنه لو توضأ بماء الورد لا يصح وضوؤه

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa argues that the verse establishes water as purifying and this status persists after mixing changes it.
rows.anchor: دلت الآية على كون الماء مطهرا والأصل في الثابت بقاؤه

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: He argues that 5:6 commands washing without qualification and changed water fulfills that command.
rows.anchor: أمر بمطلق الغسل وقد أتى به فوجب أن يخرج عن العهدة

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: He argues from 4:43 that changed water is still water, so a person possessing it cannot resort to tayammum.
rows.anchor: واجد هذا الماء المتغير واجد للماء لأن الماء المتغير ماء مع صفة التغير

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: He cites the Prophet's unqualified statement that seawater is purifying, permitting purification even when something is mixed into it.
rows.anchor: قوله عليه السلام في البحر : ( هو الطهور ماؤه )

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: He cites permission to use a cat's and menstruating woman's leftover water despite their saliva mixing into it.
rows.anchor: أباح الوضوء بسؤر الهرة وسؤر الحائض وإن خالطه شيء من لعابهما

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: He cites accepted ablution with muddy floodwater changed by clay, grasses, or plants as precedent for non-dominating admixtures.
rows.anchor: لا خلاف في الوضوء بماء المدر والسيول مع تغير لونه بمخالطة الطين

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري والنخعي ومالك وداود
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, al-Nakhaʿī, Mālik, and Dāwūd say water is not impure unless it changes; al-Ghazālī leans this way in the Iḥyāʾ.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الحسن البصري والنخعي ومالك وداود

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الرازي
rows.claim: Abū Bakr al-Rāzī states the Ḥanafī rule: any certainly or probably impurity-bearing water cannot be used, whether sea, well, pool, still, or flowing; pool separation concerns whether impurity reaches the far side.
rows.anchor: كل ما تيقنا فيه جزأ من النجاسة أو غلب على الظن ذلك لم يجز استعماله

rows.speaker: عبدالله بن عمر
rows.claim: A report from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar says water of forty qullahs is not made impure by anything.
rows.anchor: إذا كان الماء أربعين قلة لم ينجسه شيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that a basin should not be used by a person in major impurity unless it holds forty water-skins.
rows.anchor: الحوض لا يغتسل فيه جنب إلا أن يكون فيه أربعون غربا

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī is also named as holding the forty-water-skin threshold.
rows.anchor: وهو قول محمد بن كعب القرظي

rows.speaker: مسروق وابن سيرين
rows.claim: Masrūq and Ibn Sīrīn say abundant water is not made impure.
rows.anchor: وقال مسروق وابن سيرين : إذا كان الماء كثيرا لا ينجسه شيء

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says stagnant water resists impurity if it amounts to three qullahs.
rows.anchor: الماء الراكد لا ينجسه شيء إذا كان قدر ثلاث قلال

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī says two Hajar qullahs are not impure unless taste, smell, or color changes; less water becomes impure when impurity appears.
rows.anchor: إذا كان الماء قلتين بقلال هجر لم ينجسه إلا ما غير طعمه أو ريحه أو لونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He supports Mālik's rule that water stays pure unless taste, color, or smell changes: the verse's purity rule otherwise remains in force.
rows.anchor: ترك العمل به في الماء الذي تغير لونه أو طعمه أو ريحه لظهور النجاسة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites a report that God created water pure and nothing makes it impure except changed taste, color, or smell as explicit proof for Mālik.
rows.anchor: خلق الله الماء طهورا لا ينجسه شيء إلا ما غير طعمه أو لونه أو ريحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The face-washing command in 5:6 is fulfilled by ablution with this water, discharging the obligation.
rows.anchor: المتوضىء بهذا الماء قد غسل وجهه فيكون آتيا بما أمر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In mixtures, taste, color, and smell show which substance dominates: visible impurity means it prevails; otherwise water consumes it.
rows.anchor: فلا جرم مهما ظهر طعم النجاسة أو لونها أو ريحها كانت النجاسة غالبة على الماء

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar reportedly performed ablution from a Christian's jug despite the likely impurity of Christian vessels, relying on the absence of change.
rows.anchor: ما روي عن عمر ( أنه ) توضأ من جرة نصرانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If fixed volumes mattered, Mecca and Medina would have needed them most; no reports say the Prophet's generation measured water or guarded vessels, though children and servants handled them.
rows.anchor: لم ينقل أنهم خاضوا في تقدير المياه بالمقادير المعينة ، ولا أنهم سألوا عن كيفية حفظ المياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet let a cat drink from a vessel despite knowing it ate mice; cats also drank from their water vessels.
rows.anchor: إصغاء رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الإناء للهرة وعدم منعهم الهرة من شرب الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī treats runoff from washing impurity as pure if unchanged and impure if changed; Mālik's side asks why contact direction matters.
rows.anchor: أن غسالة النجاسات طاهرة إذا لم تتغير ونجسة إذا تغيرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People used stream edges for washing after relieving themselves; al-Shāfiʿī allows unchanged flowing water even in small amounts, so the argument questions why still water differs.
rows.anchor: كانوا يستنجون على أطراف المياه الجارية القليلة ، ولا خلاف أن مذهب الشافعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If urine enters two qullahs and they are divided, each jug is pure under al-Shāfiʿī despite traces; why differ from the same small amount entering that volume initially?
rows.anchor: إذا وقع بول في قلتين ثم فرقتا فكل كوز يؤخذ منه فهو ظاهر على قول الشافعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bathhouses had ascetics dip hands and vessels into small pools touched by clean and unclean hands; a necessary two-qullah rule would have been transmitted widely, so its absence shows it is not binding.
rows.anchor: الحمامات لم تزل في الأعصار الخالية يتوضأ فيها المتقشفون ويغمسون الأيدي والأواني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If any impurity made water impure, a threshold for enormous valleys and pools would be needed; competing volumes have no basis to prefer one.
rows.anchor: لا بد من التقدير بمقدار معين ، وقد نقلنا عن الناس تقديرات مختلفة فليس بعضها أولى من بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He calls Abū Ḥanīfa's ten-by-ten measure arbitrary.
rows.anchor: أما تقدير أبي حنيفة بعشر في عشر فمعلوم أنه مجرد تحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He challenges the two-qullah report because al-Shāfiʿī transmitted it from an unnamed informant, making it mursal and, by al-Shāfiʿī's rule, not proof.
rows.anchor: لأن الشافعي لما روى هذا الخبر ، قال أخبرني رجل فيكون الراوي مجهولا

rows.speaker: كثير من المحدثين
rows.claim: Many hadith scholars say the two-qullah report stops at Ibn ʿUmar rather than reaching the Prophet.
rows.anchor: زعم كثير من المحدثين أنه موقوف على ابن عمر رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qullah is unclear: it may mean a jug, jar, hand-carried vessel, a man's head, or a mountain summit.
rows.anchor: لأن القلة غير معلومة فإنها تصلح للكوز والجرة ولكل ما نقل باليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He lists conflicting versions: two qullahs, one, forty, two or three qullahs, and two jugs.
rows.anchor: فإنه روي ( إذا بلغ الماء قلتين ) ، وروي ( إذا بلغ قلة ) ، وروي ( أربعين قلة )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taken literally, “does not carry impurity” fails because impurity is physically carried once it enters; khabath may mean legal or natural filth, and the lexical sense is preferable.
rows.anchor: فإن الخبث إذا ورد عليه فقد حمله

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says what Arabs find repugnant is forbidden, taking khabath as natural repulsiveness; this only shows water does not become naturally foul, not that it is pure in law.
rows.anchor: قال عليه السلام : ( ما استخبثته العرب فهو حرام )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The counterargument says that if “does not carry impurity” means water is weakened by it, that effect proves impurity rather than continued purity.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الضعف تأثره به ، فيكون هذا دليلا على صيرورته نجسا لا على بقائه طاهرا

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī's defenders say he named the transmitter elsewhere and other hadith scholars identified him.
rows.anchor: فقد ذكره في سائر المواضع فخرج عن كونه مرسلا

rows.speaker: يحيى بن معين
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn calls the chain good; when told Ibn ʿUlayya stopped it at Ibn ʿUmar, he replies Ḥammād ibn Salama raised it to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: يحيى بن معين قال إنه جيد الإسناد فقيل له إن ابن علية وقفه على ابن عمر

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj specifies Hajar jars, which he says he saw; each held about two water-skins and a little more.
rows.anchor: لأن ابن جريج قال في روايته ( بقلال هجر )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The response to conflicting measures is that other proposed volumes are disregarded, leaving two qullahs as the applicable measure.
rows.anchor: على أن سائر المقادير غير معتبرة فيبقى ما ذكرناه معتبرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A response reads khabath as legal impurity, removing the objection that the report is impossible literally; scriptural speech should carry legal benefit rather than a rational reading that disables it.
rows.anchor: إذا حملناه على الخبث الشرعي اندفع ذلك ، وذلك أولى لأن حمل كلام الشرع على الفائدة الشرعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A version says two-qullah water does not become impure; the threshold then matters because a ruling tied to a condition ceases when it is absent.
rows.anchor: صح في بعض الروايات أنه قال : ( إذا كان الماء قلتين لم ينجس )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If sound, the report qualifies the broad statements in 25:48 and 5:6; the qualification must be clear, but Hajar qullahs, water-skin sizes, and conflicting wording are uncertain, so the report cannot restrict them.
rows.anchor: يقتضي تخصيص عموم قوله تعالى : { وأنزلنا من السماء ماء طهورا } وعموم قوله : { ولاكن يريد ليطهركم }

rows.speaker: القائلون بنجاسة الماء
rows.claim: Those who deem water impure cite prohibitions of filth, carrion, blood, and wine and the report about two punished graves; they infer any remaining impurity forbids use and prohibitions outweigh permissions.
rows.anchor: فحرم الله هذه الأشياء تحريما مطلقا ، ولم يفرق بين حال انفرادها واختلاطها بالماء

rows.speaker: القائلون بنجاسة الماء
rows.claim: They cite the unqualified prohibition against urinating in still water and then bathing in it, regardless of quantity.
rows.anchor: لا يبولن أحدكم في الماء الدائم ثم يغتسل فيه من الجنابة

rows.speaker: القائلون بنجاسة الماء
rows.claim: They cite washing hands three times before dipping them into a vessel after sleep as precaution against contamination that would not alter the water visibly.
rows.anchor: فليغسل يده ثلاثا قبل أن يدخلها الإناء فإنه لا يدري أين باتت يده

rows.speaker: القائلون بنجاسة الماء
rows.claim: They read the two-qullah report by implication: water below that amount must carry impurity.
rows.anchor: قوله عليه السلام : ( إذا بلغ الماء قلتين لم يحمل خبثا ) يدل بمفهومه

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik replies that a small liquid impurity may lose its properties in water; it is not established that it remains unchanged rather than transforming.
rows.anchor: فلم قلتم إن تلك النجاسة بقيت ، ولم لا يجوز أن يقال إنها انقلبت عن صفتها

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: He says the still-water ban may prevent people from drinking it out of natural revulsion, not establish a purity rule.
rows.anchor: لعل النهي إنما كان لأنه ربما شربه إنسان وذلك مما ينفر طبعه عنه

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: The hand-washing command is unanimously recommended, so it cannot establish obligatory contamination; even if obligatory, its stated reason is unproven.
rows.anchor: فقد أجمعنا على أن هذا الأمر استحباب ، فالمرتب عليه كيف يكون أمر

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: The two-qullah proof rests on implication, whereas the cited texts state their rules explicitly and thus take precedence.
rows.anchor: فهو تمسك بالمفهوم والنصوص التي ذكرناها منطوقة والمنطوق راجح على المفهوم

rows.speaker: الأصم والأوزاعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm and al-Awzāʿī permit ablution with every liquid.
rows.anchor: قال الأصم والأوزاعي يجوز الوضوء بجميع المائعات

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa permits ablution with date wine while traveling.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة يجوز الوضوء بنبيذ التمر في السفر

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa also allows removing physical impurity with liquids that remove its substance.
rows.anchor: تجوز إزالة النجاسة بجميع المائعات التي تزيل أعيان النجاسات

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī holds that all purification is restricted to water.
rows.anchor: الطهورية مختصة بالماء على الإطلاق

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: For ritual impurity, al-Shāfiʿī argues from 4:43 that if vinegar or date wine replaced water, tayammum would not be required when water is absent.
rows.anchor: أوجب التيمم عند عدم الماء ، ولو جاز الوضوء بالخل أو نبيذ التمر

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: For physical impurity, if vinegar removed it, it would be a purifier; a hadith would then imply ritual purification by vinegar too, but that is not accepted, so purification is water-specific.
rows.anchor: الخل لو أفاد طهارة الخبث لكان طهورا لأنه لا معنى للطهور إلا المطهر
